A landlord or their agent may not charge an application or similar fee to lease or sublease a residential rental property that exceeds $50, subject to annual CPI adjustments.
No residential landlord may evict or fail to renew a lease, whether written or oral, without good cause, and the landlord must prove in court that grounds for eviction exist.
When a building is converted to a condominium, cooperative, or fee simple ownership, rents may not be increased solely to cover costs resulting from the conversion.
Landlords converting properties to condominiums or cooperatives must serve a three-year Notice to Quit before filing for eviction.
Landlords are allowed to charge the tenant for the cost of the credit report and may request reasonable rental application fees or employment verification.

A landlord may file an eviction suit if a tenant fails to pay a rent increase, provided the rent increase is not unconscionable and complies with all other laws or municipal ordinances, including rent control, and a Notice to Quit is served at least one month prior.
Landlords may evict for habitual late payment of rent after serving a Notice to Cease and a one-month Notice to Quit.
Tenants evicted for illegal occupancy are entitled to relocation assistance equal to six times their monthly rent, payable by the landlord at least five days before removal.

Certain senior citizens and recipients of specific governmental pensions, disability benefits, or assistance must be given a five-business-day grace period for rent due on the first of the month without delinquency or late charges assessed.
The maximum security deposit a landlord can collect from a tenant cannot exceed one and one-half times one month's rent.

Landlords and rental agencies are prohibited from refusing to rent or discriminating in housing units based on race, creed, color, national origin, ancestry, sex, marital status, civil union status, domestic partnership status, familial status, affectional or sexual orientation, gender identity or expression, mental and physical disability, nationality, or source of lawful income.

Landlords receiving security deposit money for ten or less units must deposit the funds in an insured bank or savings and loan association located in New Jersey in an interest-bearing account. Landlords with 10 or more units have the option of investing in an insured money market fund or a variable rate account in a New Jersey bank. All interest or earnings belong to the tenant and must be paid in cash or credited toward rent.

Within 30 days after the termination of a tenancy, a landlord must return the security deposit plus interest less allowable deductions. If a landlord fails to return the deposit within 30 days or wrongfully withholds an amount, the tenant may sue for double the amount plus court costs and reasonable attorney's fees.

When a new owner of a foreclosed property makes a bona fide monetary offer to induce a tenant to vacate, they are prohibited from using pressure tactics, including increasing rent in excess of any applicable rent control ordinance or, if not subject to rent control, imposing an unreasonable or unconscionable rent increase.
Newly constructed multiple dwellings are exempt from any local rent control ordinances for a period of 30 years following completion of construction.
Landlords may evict tenants who refuse reasonable, substantial changes to lease terms upon expiration, provided a one-month Notice to Quit is served.

Unknown: owner type is not in the supplied data. Landlords of residential rental properties, excluding owner-occupied two or three-family dwellings, motels, hotels, or transient/seasonal units, must have good cause to refuse to renew a lease.

Landlords are prohibited from evicting, altering lease terms, or refusing to renew a lease in reprisal for a tenant exercising civil rights, such as enforcing lease rights or complaining to government authorities.

Landlords seeking to permanently retire a building from residential use must serve a Notice to Quit at least 18 months prior to filing for eviction, and no action may be taken until the lease expires.

Landlords are prohibited from discriminating against tenants or purchasers based on their source of lawful income or source of lawful rent or mortgage payment, including the use of Section 8 HUD vouchers.

Compliance with municipal rent control regulations is entirely voluntary and uncoerced after six months from the date of initial adoption, and property owners may decline to have their property subjected to the regulation.

Municipal rent control regulations cannot include the regulation of occupancy, services, evictions, condominium conversion, or removal of properties, and cannot apply to units owned by someone owning less than ten rental units or units with a fair market rent exceeding $400.

A municipality adopting rent control must compensate owners of rent-controlled units for the difference between the unit's fair market rent and its below-market rent-controlled rent using the municipality's general funds.

Cities and towns are prohibited from enacting, maintaining, or enforcing rent control of any kind, unless they accept Chapter 40P and adopt voluntary regulations meeting specific statutory conditions.

Estates at will may be determined by either party by giving three months' notice in writing, or an interval equal to the payment period or thirty days (whichever is longer) if rent is payable at periods of less than three months.

At or prior to the commencement of any tenancy, a lessor or agent may not require payments exceeding the first full month's rent, last full month's rent, a security deposit equal to the first month's rent, and the purchase and installation cost for a key and lock.

If a lessor fails to properly deposit security funds, transfer them to a successor, or return them to the tenant, the tenant is entitled to damages equal to three times the security deposit amount plus 5% interest, court costs, and attorney's fees.
Any lease provision that conflicts with the security deposit requirements or attempts to waive tenant rights under this section is void and unenforceable as a matter of public policy.
The security deposit provisions do not apply to vacation or recreational rentals with a duration of 100 days or less.

Landlords are prohibited from threatening or taking reprisals against residential tenants for reporting code violations, joining a tenants' union, or pursuing legal rights. Any waiver of the statutory protections against landlord reprisals contained in any lease or other rental agreement shall be void and unenforceable.
A licensed broker or salesperson may only collect a fee from the party (lessor or tenant) who originally engaged and entered into a contract with them.

A landlord must provide a specific form alongside any notice to quit for nonpayment of rent, which includes repayment agreements and information on rental assistance and legal rights. Courts cannot accept an eviction filing for nonpayment of rent without proof that this form was delivered to the tenant.

Cities and towns are prohibited from enacting, maintaining, or enforcing rent control of any kind, unless they accept Chapter 40P and adopt voluntary regulations meeting specific statutory conditions.

Estates at will may be determined by either party by giving three months' notice in writing, or an interval equal to the payment period or thirty days (whichever is longer) if rent is payable at periods of less than three months.

In case of neglect or refusal to pay rent, a fourteen days' notice to quit in writing is sufficient to determine the tenancy, provided that a tenant who has not received a similar notice within the preceding twelve months may cure the default by paying or tendering the full amount of rent due within ten days of receipt.

At or prior to the commencement of any tenancy, a lessor or agent may not require payments exceeding the first full month's rent, last full month's rent, a security deposit equal to the first month's rent, and the purchase and installation cost for a key and lock.

If a lessor fails to properly deposit security funds, transfer them to a successor, or return them to the tenant, the tenant is entitled to damages equal to three times the security deposit amount plus 5% interest, court costs, and attorney's fees.
Any lease provision that conflicts with the security deposit requirements or attempts to waive tenant rights under this section is void and unenforceable as a matter of public policy.
The security deposit provisions do not apply to vacation or recreational rentals with a duration of 100 days or less.

Landlords are prohibited from threatening or taking reprisals against residential tenants for reporting code violations, joining a tenants' union, or pursuing legal rights. Receipt of a notice of termination, rent increase, or substantial alteration in tenancy terms within six months of such tenant activity creates a rebuttable presumption of reprisal.
Any waiver of the statutory protections against landlord reprisals contained in any lease or other rental agreement shall be void and unenforceable.
A licensed broker or salesperson may only collect a fee from the party (lessor or tenant) who originally engaged and entered into a contract with them.

A landlord must provide a specific form alongside any notice to quit for nonpayment of rent, which includes repayment agreements and information on rental assistance and legal rights. Courts cannot accept an eviction filing for nonpayment of rent without proof that this form was delivered to the tenant.

A0246.explanation: Landlords may only charge a maximum of one month's rent for unfurnished and furnished units, with an exception for certain small landlords who may charge up to two months' rent.

It is unlawful for any person to use or distribute a common pricing algorithm as part of a contract, combination in the form of a trust, or conspiracy to restrain trade or commerce, or to coerce another person to set or adopt a recommended price or commercial term recommended by a common pricing algorithm for the same or similar products or services.
After a tenant has occupied a property for 12 months, the owner must have just cause to terminate the tenancy and must state that cause in the written notice.
If an owner terminates a tenancy for a no-fault just cause, they must provide relocation assistance equal to one month's rent or waive the final month's rent.
After a tenant has occupied a property for 12 months (or 24 months if only one tenant has occupied it), a landlord must provide a statement of cause in any notice to terminate a tenancy.

An owner of residential real property shall not increase the gross rental rate for a dwelling or unit by more than 5 percent plus the percentage change in the cost of living, or 10 percent, whichever is lower, over any 12-month period.
A landlord shall not demand or receive a security deposit in excess of one month's rent, in addition to the first month's rent.
Landlords must return the security deposit and provide an itemized statement of deductions within 21 calendar days after the tenant has vacated the premises.

Landlords or their successors who act in bad faith regarding the retention of a security deposit or the demand for replacement security may be liable for statutory damages of up to twice the amount of the security deposit, in addition to actual damages.
A lease or rental agreement is prohibited from including any provision that characterizes a security deposit as nonrefundable.

The application screening fee must not exceed the actual out-of-pocket costs of gathering information and the reasonable value of the landlord's time, with a maximum cap of $30 per applicant, subject to annual CPI adjustments.

Landlords may not charge a screening fee if they know or should know no unit is available, and may only charge if they offer a compliant screening process (either first-come-first-served or a full refund policy for non-selected applicants).
Housing providers must evaluate the aggregate income of all persons residing together using the same standards applied to married persons.
For tenants with government rent subsidies, housing providers must base financial or income eligibility standards only on the portion of rent the tenant is responsible for paying.
For tenants with government rent subsidies, housing providers must allow applicants to provide alternative evidence of their ability to pay rent instead of relying solely on credit history.
Landlords must provide 30 days' written advance notice for rent increases of less than 10%.

If a residential rental property is re-rented within five years after a no-fault eviction under specific sections, the landlord must first offer to lease the unit back to the displaced tenant if the tenant timely requested it in writing and provided contact information.

Prior to making a buyout offer, landlords must provide each tenant a written disclosure stating their right not to enter into the agreement, consult an attorney, refuse future offers, and receive relocation assistance, among other mandated notices.
A landlord is prohibited from terminating a residential tenancy without establishing at-fault or no-fault just cause as defined by the ordinance.

A landlord of a residential rental property subject to this Division must provide written notice in no less than 12-point font regarding rent limits, local just cause termination rules, and senior or disabled tenant protections, and include a copy of the Tenant Protection Guide.

For no-fault just cause terminations, landlords must provide relocation assistance either via direct payment equal to two months of actual rent (or three months if the tenant is a senior or disabled) or through an equivalent rent waiver for the final months of tenancy.

Buyout agreements must be in writing, provide a copy to each tenant at signing, include specific bold statutory notices in at least 14-point font, be provided in translated versions if negotiations occurred in a non-English language, and be for an amount greater than the required relocation assistance.
Landlords are prohibited from retaliating against a tenant for exercising any right provided by or seeking enforcement of the division.
Any buyout agreement for less than the amount of relocation assistance owed to the tenant violates the division and is void.

Landlords are prohibited from terminating tenancies without just cause and must provide relocation assistance for no-fault evictions.

All notices to terminate a tenancy for rental units subject to the RSO must be filed with the Los Angeles Housing Department within three business days of service on the tenant.
A landlord may collect 1/12 of 50% of the annual Systematic Code Enforcement Fee from the tenant of the rental unit per month.

Landlords of units subject to the Rent Stabilization Ordinance are limited to an annual rent increase of 3% for the period of July 1, 2025, through June 30, 2026.

Landlords may elect to pay monetary relocation benefits through an escrow account established within the required 15-day period, which must disburse funds for actual relocation expenses within three working days of receiving a request.

A0249.explanation: Unknown: owner type is not in the supplied data. A housing provider is prohibited from inquiring about an applicant's criminal record or requiring an application that includes such inquiries until after a conditional offer of housing has been made.

Unknown: owner type is not in the supplied data. Housing providers are prohibited from evaluating applicants based on arrests not resulting in conviction, expunged convictions, pardoned convictions, vacated convictions, juvenile adjudications, or sealed records.

Unknown: owner type is not in the supplied data. Housing providers are prohibited from requiring applicants to submit to drug or alcohol tests or requesting consent to obtain information from drug abuse treatment facilities.
A landlord or their agent may not charge an application or similar fee to lease or sublease a residential rental property that exceeds $50, subject to annual CPI adjustments.
No residential landlord may evict or fail to renew a lease, whether written or oral, without good cause, and the landlord must prove in court that grounds for eviction exist.
When a building is converted to a condominium, cooperative, or fee simple ownership, rents may not be increased solely to cover costs resulting from the conversion.
Landlords converting properties to condominiums or cooperatives must serve a three-year Notice to Quit before filing for eviction.
Landlords are allowed to charge the tenant for the cost of the credit report and may request reasonable rental application fees or employment verification.

A landlord may file an eviction suit if a tenant fails to pay a rent increase, provided the rent increase is not unconscionable and complies with all other laws or municipal ordinances, including rent control, and a Notice to Quit is served at least one month prior.
Landlords may evict for habitual late payment of rent after serving a Notice to Cease and a one-month Notice to Quit.
Tenants evicted for illegal occupancy are entitled to relocation assistance equal to six times their monthly rent, payable by the landlord at least five days before removal.

Certain senior citizens and recipients of specific governmental pensions, disability benefits, or assistance must be given a five-business-day grace period for rent due on the first of the month without delinquency or late charges assessed.
The maximum security deposit a landlord can collect from a tenant cannot exceed one and one-half times one month's rent.

Landlords and rental agencies are prohibited from refusing to rent or discriminating in housing units based on race, creed, color, national origin, ancestry, sex, marital status, civil union status, domestic partnership status, familial status, affectional or sexual orientation, gender identity or expression, mental and physical disability, nationality, or source of lawful income.

Landlords receiving security deposit money for ten or less units must deposit the funds in an insured bank or savings and loan association located in New Jersey in an interest-bearing account. Landlords with 10 or more units have the option of investing in an insured money market fund or a variable rate account in a New Jersey bank. All interest or earnings belong to the tenant and must be paid in cash or credited toward rent.

Within 30 days after the termination of a tenancy, a landlord must return the security deposit plus interest less allowable deductions. If a landlord fails to return the deposit within 30 days or wrongfully withholds an amount, the tenant may sue for double the amount plus court costs and reasonable attorney's fees.

When a new owner of a foreclosed property makes a bona fide monetary offer to induce a tenant to vacate, they are prohibited from using pressure tactics, including increasing rent in excess of any applicable rent control ordinance or, if not subject to rent control, imposing an unreasonable or unconscionable rent increase.
Newly constructed multiple dwellings are exempt from any local rent control ordinances for a period of 30 years following completion of construction.
Landlords may evict tenants who refuse reasonable, substantial changes to lease terms upon expiration, provided a one-month Notice to Quit is served.

Unknown: owner type is not in the supplied data. Landlords of residential rental properties, excluding owner-occupied two or three-family dwellings, motels, hotels, or transient/seasonal units, must have good cause to refuse to renew a lease.

Landlords are prohibited from evicting, altering lease terms, or refusing to renew a lease in reprisal for a tenant exercising civil rights, such as enforcing lease rights or complaining to government authorities.

Landlords seeking to permanently retire a building from residential use must serve a Notice to Quit at least 18 months prior to filing for eviction, and no action may be taken until the lease expires.

Landlords are prohibited from discriminating against tenants or purchasers based on their source of lawful income or source of lawful rent or mortgage payment, including the use of Section 8 HUD vouchers.

A landlord shall not demand or receive a security deposit in excess of one month's rent, in addition to the first month's rent.

Rent increases can only take effect at the expiration or termination of a lease or periodic lease, and any increase exceeding authorized chapter provisions is void.

Landlords may not request or receive a percentage rent increase greater than 5% or the percentage difference in the consumer price index between three months prior to lease expiration and three months prior to lease commencement, whichever is less.

Landlords must obtain Rent Leveling and Stabilization Board approval before imposing a capital improvement rent surcharge, and base rents shall under no circumstances be increased by an amount greater than 33 1/3% due to a capital improvement surcharge in any one twelve-month period.

Landlords who cannot meet operating expenses or do not make a fair return on investment may appeal to the Rent Leveling and Stabilization Board for a hardship rental increase, provided they obtain prior Board approval and serve notice to each tenant at least 20 days before the hearing.

Landlords seeking to increase rent by more than 10% upon lease renewal year over year must provide specific disclosures to existing tenants, including cost itemizations, algorithmic pricing usage statements, tenant legal rights notices, and Hoboken Division of Housing contact info.

The maximum security deposit a landlord can collect from a tenant cannot exceed one and one-half times one month's rent.

Landlords receiving security deposit money for ten or less units must deposit the funds in an insured bank or savings and loan association located in New Jersey in an interest-bearing account. Landlords may evict tenants who refuse reasonable, substantial changes to lease terms upon expiration, provided a one-month Notice to Quit is served.

A landlord is prohibited from terminating a residential tenancy without establishing at-fault or no-fault just cause as defined by the ordinance.

For no-fault just cause terminations, landlords must provide relocation assistance either via direct payment equal to two months of actual rent (or three months if the tenant is a senior or disabled) or through an equivalent rent waiver for the final months of tenancy.

Buyout agreements must be in writing, provide a copy to each tenant at signing, include specific bold statutory notices in at least 14-point font, be provided in translated versions if negotiations occurred in a non-English language, and be for an amount greater than the required relocation assistance.
Landlords are prohibited from retaliating against a tenant for exercising any right provided by or seeking enforcement of the division.
Any buyout agreement for less than the amount of relocation assistance owed to the tenant violates the division and is void.

Compliance with municipal rent control regulations is entirely voluntary and uncoerced after six months from the date of initial adoption, and property owners may decline to have their property subjected to the regulation.

Municipal rent control regulations cannot include the regulation of occupancy, services, evictions, condominium conversion, or removal of properties, and cannot apply to units owned by someone owning less than ten rental units or units with a fair market rent exceeding $400.

A municipality adopting rent control must compensate owners of rent-controlled units for the difference between the unit's fair market rent and its below-market rent-controlled rent using the municipality's general funds.

Cities and towns are prohibited from enacting, maintaining, or enforcing rent control of any kind, unless they accept Chapter 40P and adopt voluntary regulations meeting specific statutory conditions.

In case of neglect or refusal to pay rent, a fourteen days' notice to quit in writing is sufficient to determine the tenancy, provided that a tenant who has not received a similar notice within the preceding twelve months may cure the default by paying or tendering the full amount of rent due within ten days of receipt.

At or prior to the commencement of any tenancy, a lessor or agent may not require payments exceeding the first full month's rent, last full month's rent, a security deposit equal to the first month's rent, and the purchase and installation cost for a key and lock.

If a lessor fails to properly deposit security funds, transfer them to a successor, or return them to the tenant, the tenant is entitled to damages equal to three times the security deposit amount plus 5% interest, court costs, and attorney's fees.
Any lease provision that conflicts with the security deposit requirements or attempts to waive tenant rights under this section is void and unenforceable as a matter of public policy.
The security deposit provisions do not apply to vacation or recreational rentals with a duration of 100 days or less.

Landlords may not request or receive a percentage rent increase greater than 5% or the percentage difference in the consumer price index between three months prior to lease expiration and three months prior to lease commencement, whichever is less.

Landlords must obtain Rent Leveling and Stabilization Board approval before imposing a capital improvement rent surcharge, and base rents shall under no circumstances be increased by an amount greater than 33 1/3% due to a capital improvement surcharge in any one twelve-month period.

Landlords are allowed to charge the tenant for the cost of the credit report and may request reasonable rental application fees or employment verification.

Tenants evicted for illegal occupancy are entitled to relocation assistance equal to six times their monthly rent, payable by the landlord at least five days before removal.

Landlords receiving security deposit money for ten or less units must deposit the funds in an insured bank or savings and loan association located in New Jersey in an interest-bearing account. Landlords with 10 or more units have the option of investing in an insured money market fund or a variable rate account in a New Jersey bank. All interest or earnings belong to the tenant and must be paid in cash or credited toward rent.

Within 30 days after the termination of a tenancy, a landlord must return the security deposit plus interest less allowable deductions. If a landlord fails to return the deposit within 30 days or wrongfully withholds an amount, the tenant may sue for double the amount plus court costs and reasonable attorney's fees.

When a new owner of a foreclosed property makes a bona fide monetary offer to induce a tenant to vacate, they are prohibited from using pressure tactics, including increasing rent in excess of any applicable rent control ordinance or, if not subject to rent control, imposing an unreasonable or unconscionable rent increase.
Newly constructed multiple dwellings are exempt from any local rent control ordinances for a period of 30 years following completion of construction.
Landlords may evict tenants who refuse reasonable, substantial changes to lease terms upon expiration, provided a one-month Notice to Quit is served.

Compliance with municipal rent control regulations is entirely voluntary and uncoerced after six months from the date of initial adoption, and property owners may decline to have their property subjected to the regulation.

A municipality adopting rent control must compensate owners of rent-controlled units for the difference between the unit's fair market rent and its below-market rent-controlled rent using the municipality's general funds.

Cities and towns are prohibited from enacting, maintaining, or enforcing rent control of any kind, unless they accept Chapter 40P and adopt voluntary regulations meeting specific statutory conditions.

Estates at will may be determined by either party by giving three months' notice in writing, or an interval equal to the payment period or thirty days (whichever is longer) if rent is payable at periods of less than three months.

In case of neglect or refusal to pay rent, a fourteen days' notice to quit in writing is sufficient to determine the tenancy, provided that a tenant who has not received a similar notice within the preceding twelve months may cure the default by paying or tendering the full amount of rent due within ten days of receipt.

At or prior to the commencement of any tenancy, a lessor or agent may not require payments exceeding the first full month's rent, last full month's rent, a security deposit equal to the first month's rent, and the purchase and installation cost for a key and lock.

If a lessor fails to properly deposit security funds, transfer them to a successor, or return them to the tenant, the tenant is entitled to damages equal to three times the security deposit amount plus 5% interest, court costs, and attorney's fees.
Any lease provision that conflicts with the security deposit requirements or attempts to waive tenant rights under this section is void and unenforceable as a matter of public policy.
The security deposit provisions do not apply to vacation or recreational rentals with a duration of 100 days or less.

Any waiver of the statutory protections against landlord reprisals contained in any lease or other rental agreement shall be void and unenforceable.
A licensed broker or salesperson may only collect a fee from the party (lessor or tenant) who originally engaged and entered into a contract with them.

Rent increases can only take effect at the expiration or termination of a lease or periodic lease, and any increase exceeding authorized chapter provisions is void.

Landlords may not request or receive a percentage rent increase greater than 5% or the percentage difference in the consumer price index between three months prior to lease expiration and three months prior to lease commencement, whichever is less.

Landlords must obtain Rent Leveling and Stabilization Board approval before imposing a capital improvement rent surcharge, and base rents shall under no circumstances be increased by an amount greater than 33 1/3% due to a capital improvement surcharge in any one twelve-month period.

Landlords who cannot meet operating expenses or do not make a fair return on investment may appeal to the Rent Leveling and Stabilization Board for a hardship rental increase, provided they obtain prior Board approval and serve notice to each tenant at least 20 days before the hearing.

Tenants may apply to the Rent Leveling and Stabilization Board for a decrease in rent when services, care, or maintenance decline in any dwelling, after serving notice on the landlord and allowing at least 20 days to elapse before a hearing.

Landlords seeking to increase rent by more than 10% upon lease renewal year over year must provide specific disclosures to existing tenants, including cost itemizations, algorithmic pricing usage statements, tenant legal rights notices, and Hoboken Division of Housing contact info.

Landlords are prohibited from using software, algorithms, or data-sharing platforms to collect and analyze nonpublic competitor information to coordinate, recommend, or implement rental prices, lease terms, or occupancy levels among competing lessors.

Tenants evicted for illegal occupancy are entitled to relocation assistance equal to six times their monthly rent, payable by the landlord at least five days before removal.

Certain senior citizens and recipients of specific governmental pensions, disability benefits, or assistance must be given a five-business-day grace period for rent due on the first of the month without delinquency or late charges assessed.
The maximum security deposit a landlord can collect from a tenant cannot exceed one and one-half times one month's rent.

Within 30 days after the termination of a tenancy, a landlord must return the security deposit plus interest less allowable deductions. Newly constructed multiple dwellings are exempt from any local rent control ordinances for a period of 30 years following completion of construction.
Landlords may evict tenants who refuse reasonable, substantial changes to lease terms upon expiration, provided a one-month Notice to Quit is served.

Landlords seeking to permanently retire a building from residential use must serve a Notice to Quit at least 18 months prior to filing for eviction, and no action may be taken until the lease expires.

Landlords are prohibited from discriminating against tenants or purchasers based on their source of lawful income or source of lawful rent or mortgage payment, including the use of Section 8 HUD vouchers.

At or prior to the commencement of any tenancy, a lessor or agent may not require payments exceeding the first full month's rent, last full month's rent, a security deposit equal to the first month's rent, and the purchase and installation cost for a key and lock.

Any lease provision that conflicts with the security deposit requirements or attempts to waive tenant rights under this section is void and unenforceable as a matter of public policy.
The security deposit provisions do not apply to vacation or recreational rentals with a duration of 100 days or less.

Tenants evicted for illegal occupancy are entitled to relocation assistance equal to six times their monthly rent, payable by the landlord at least five days before removal.

Certain senior citizens and recipients of specific governmental pensions, disability benefits, or assistance must be given a five-business-day grace period for rent due on the first of the month without delinquency or late charges assessed.
The maximum security deposit a landlord can collect from a tenant cannot exceed one and one-half times one month's rent.

Landlords and rental agencies are prohibited from refusing to rent or discriminating in housing units based on race, creed, color, national origin, ancestry, sex, marital status, civil union status, domestic partnership status, familial status, affectional or sexual orientation, gender identity or expression, mental and physical disability, nationality, or source of lawful income.

Landlords receiving security deposit money for ten or less units must deposit the funds in an insured bank or savings and loan association located in New Jersey in an interest-bearing account. Landlords with 10 or more units have the option of investing in an insured money market fund or a variable rate account in a New Jersey bank. All interest or earnings belong to the tenant and must be paid in cash or credited toward rent.

Within 30 days after the termination of a tenancy, a landlord must return the security deposit plus interest less allowable deductions. If a landlord fails to return the deposit within 30 days or wrongfully withholds an amount, the tenant may sue for double the amount plus court costs and reasonable attorney's fees.

When a new owner of a foreclosed property makes a bona fide monetary offer to induce a tenant to vacate, they are prohibited from using pressure tactics, including increasing rent in excess of any applicable rent control ordinance or, if not subject to rent control, imposing an unreasonable or unconscionable rent increase.
Newly constructed multiple dwellings are exempt from any local rent control ordinances for a period of 30 years following completion of construction.
Landlords may evict tenants who refuse reasonable, substantial changes to lease terms upon expiration, provided a one-month Notice to Quit is served.

Unknown: owner type is not in the supplied data. Landlords of residential rental properties, excluding owner-occupied two or three-family dwellings, motels, hotels, or transient/seasonal units, must have good cause to refuse to renew a lease.

Landlords are prohibited from evicting, altering lease terms, or refusing to renew a lease in reprisal for a tenant exercising civil rights, such as enforcing lease rights or complaining to government authorities.

Landlords seeking to permanently retire a building from residential use must serve a Notice to Quit at least 18 months prior to filing for eviction, and no action may be taken until the lease expires.

Landlords are prohibited from discriminating against tenants or purchasers based on their source of lawful income or source of lawful rent or mortgage payment, including the use of Section 8 HUD vouchers.

Not yet effective as of 2026-10-01. It is unlawful for rental property owners to use coordinators for rent setting, for coordinators to facilitate agreements that restrict competition, or for any person to perform a coordinating function that uses algorithms to process competitively sensitive information to set rental prices.

Rent increases can only take effect at the expiration or termination of a lease or periodic lease, and any increase exceeding authorized chapter provisions is void.

Landlords may not request or receive a percentage rent increase greater than 5% or the percentage difference in the consumer price index between three months prior to lease expiration and three months prior to lease commencement, whichever is less.

Landlords must obtain Rent Leveling and Stabilization Board approval before imposing a capital improvement rent surcharge, and base rents shall under no circumstances be increased by an amount greater than 33 1/3% due to a capital improvement surcharge in any one twelve-month period.

Landlords who cannot meet operating expenses or do not make a fair return on investment may appeal to the Rent Leveling and Stabilization Board for a hardship rental increase, provided they obtain prior Board approval and serve notice to each tenant at least 20 days before the hearing.

Tenants may apply to the Rent Leveling and Stabilization Board for a decrease in rent when services, care, or maintenance decline in any dwelling, after serving notice on the landlord and allowing at least 20 days to elapse before a hearing.

Landlords seeking to increase rent by more than 10% upon lease renewal year over year must provide specific disclosures to existing tenants, including cost itemizations, algorithmic pricing usage statements, tenant legal rights notices, and Hoboken Division of Housing contact info.

Landlords are prohibited from using software, algorithms, or data-sharing platforms to collect and analyze nonpublic competitor information to coordinate, recommend, or implement rental prices, lease terms, or occupancy levels among competing lessors.

A0309.explanation: Landlords may only charge a maximum of one month's rent for unfurnished and furnished units, with an exception for certain small landlords who may charge up to two months' rent.

After a tenant has occupied a property for 12 months, the owner must have just cause to terminate the tenancy and must state that cause in the written notice.
If an owner terminates a tenancy for a no-fault just cause, they must provide relocation assistance equal to one month's rent or waive the final month's rent.
After a tenant has occupied a property for 12 months (or 24 months if only one tenant has occupied it), a landlord must provide a statement of cause in any notice to terminate a tenancy.

An owner of residential real property shall not increase the gross rental rate for a dwelling or unit by more than 5 percent plus the percentage change in the cost of living, or 10 percent, whichever is lower, over any 12-month period.
A landlord shall not demand or receive a security deposit in excess of one month's rent, in addition to the first month's rent.
Landlords must return the security deposit and provide an itemized statement of deductions within 21 calendar days after the tenant has vacated the premises.

Landlords or their successors who act in bad faith regarding the retention of a security deposit or the demand for replacement security may be liable for statutory damages of up to twice the amount of the security deposit, in addition to actual damages.
A lease or rental agreement is prohibited from including any provision that characterizes a security deposit as nonrefundable.

The application screening fee must not exceed the actual out-of-pocket costs of gathering information and the reasonable value of the landlord's time, with a maximum cap of $30 per applicant, subject to annual CPI adjustments.

Landlords may not charge a screening fee if they know or should know no unit is available, and may only charge if they offer a compliant screening process (either first-come-first-served or a full refund policy for non-selected applicants).
Housing providers must evaluate the aggregate income of all persons residing together using the same standards applied to married persons.
For tenants with government rent subsidies, housing providers must base financial or income eligibility standards only on the portion of rent the tenant is responsible for paying.
For tenants with government rent subsidies, housing providers must allow applicants to provide alternative evidence of their ability to pay rent instead of relying solely on credit history.

Landlords are prohibited from terminating tenancies without just cause and must provide relocation assistance for no-fault evictions.
Rent may be increased once every 12 months by the allowable rent increase percentage. Landlords are prohibited from including an additional percentage increase for utilities.
All notices to terminate a tenancy for rental units subject to the RSO must be filed with the Los Angeles Housing Department within three business days of service on the tenant.
A landlord may collect 1/12 of 50% of the annual Systematic Code Enforcement Fee from the tenant of the rental unit per month.
Landlords must provide 30 days' written advance notice for rent increases of less than 10%.
Landlords of units subject to the Rent Stabilization Ordinance are limited to an annual rent increase of 3% for the period of July 1, 2025, through June 30, 2026.
Beginning February 2, 2026, landlords are prohibited from including any additional percentage increase for utilities in the rent.

Landlords may elect to pay monetary relocation benefits through an escrow account established within the required 15-day period, which must disburse funds for actual relocation expenses within three working days of receiving a request.

Compliance with municipal rent control regulations is entirely voluntary and uncoerced after six months from the date of initial adoption, and property owners may decline to have their property subjected to the regulation.

Municipal rent control regulations cannot include the regulation of occupancy, services, evictions, condominium conversion, or removal of properties, and cannot apply to units owned by someone owning less than ten rental units or units with a fair market rent exceeding $400.

A municipality adopting rent control must compensate owners of rent-controlled units for the difference between the unit's fair market rent and its below-market rent-controlled rent using the municipality's general funds.

Cities and towns are prohibited from enacting, maintaining, or enforcing rent control of any kind, unless they accept Chapter 40P and adopt voluntary regulations meeting specific statutory conditions.

Estates at will may be determined by either party by giving three months' notice in writing, or an interval equal to the payment period or thirty days (whichever is longer) if rent is payable at periods of less than three months.

In case of neglect or refusal to pay rent, a fourteen days' notice to quit in writing is sufficient to determine the tenancy, provided that a tenant who has not received a similar notice within the preceding twelve months may cure the default by paying or tendering the full amount of rent due within ten days of receipt.

At or prior to the commencement of any tenancy, a lessor or agent may not require payments exceeding the first full month's rent, last full month's rent, a security deposit equal to the first month's rent, and the purchase and installation cost for a key and lock.

If a lessor fails to properly deposit security funds, transfer them to a successor, or return them to the tenant, the tenant is entitled to damages equal to three times the security deposit amount plus 5% interest, court costs, and attorney's fees.
Any lease provision that conflicts with the security deposit requirements or attempts to waive tenant rights under this section is void and unenforceable as a matter of public policy.
The security deposit provisions do not apply to vacation or recreational rentals with a duration of 100 days or less.

Landlords are prohibited from threatening or taking reprisals against residential tenants for reporting code violations, joining a tenants' union, or pursuing legal rights. Receipt of a notice of termination, rent increase, or substantial alteration in tenancy terms within six months of such tenant activity creates a rebuttable presumption of reprisal.
Any waiver of the statutory protections against landlord reprisals contained in any lease or other rental agreement shall be void and unenforceable.
A licensed broker or salesperson may only collect a fee from the party (lessor or tenant) who originally engaged and entered into a contract with them.

A landlord must provide a specific form alongside any notice to quit for nonpayment of rent, which includes repayment agreements and information on rental assistance and legal rights. Courts cannot accept an eviction filing for nonpayment of rent without proof that this form was delivered to the tenant.

Landlords may evict for habitual late payment of rent after serving a Notice to Cease and a one-month Notice to Quit.

Certain senior citizens and recipients of specific governmental pensions, disability benefits, or assistance must be given a five-business-day grace period for rent due on the first of the month without delinquency or late charges assessed.
The maximum security deposit a landlord can collect from a tenant cannot exceed one and one-half times one month's rent.

Landlords and rental agencies are prohibited from refusing to rent or discriminating in housing units based on race, creed, color, national origin, ancestry, sex, marital status, civil union status, domestic partnership status, familial status, affectional or sexual orientation, gender identity or expression, mental and physical disability, nationality, or source of lawful income.

Landlords receiving security deposit money for ten or less units must deposit the funds in an insured bank or savings and loan association located in New Jersey in an interest-bearing account. Landlords with 10 or more units have the option of investing in an insured money market fund or a variable rate account in a New Jersey bank. All interest or earnings belong to the tenant and must be paid in cash or credited toward rent.

Within 30 days after the termination of a tenancy, a landlord must return the security deposit plus interest less allowable deductions. If a landlord fails to return the deposit within 30 days or wrongfully withholds an amount, the tenant may sue for double the amount plus court costs and reasonable attorney's fees.

When a new owner of a foreclosed property makes a bona fide monetary offer to induce a tenant to vacate, they are prohibited from using pressure tactics, including increasing rent in excess of any applicable rent control ordinance or, if not subject to rent control, imposing an unreasonable or unconscionable rent increase.
Newly constructed multiple dwellings are exempt from any local rent control ordinances for a period of 30 years following completion of construction.
Landlords may evict tenants who refuse reasonable, substantial changes to lease terms upon expiration, provided a one-month Notice to Quit is served.

Landlords are prohibited from discriminating against tenants or purchasers based on their source of lawful income or source of lawful rent or mortgage payment, including the use of Section 8 HUD vouchers.

After a tenant has occupied a property for 12 months (or 24 months if only one tenant has occupied it), a landlord must provide a statement of cause in any notice to terminate a tenancy.

The application screening fee must not exceed the actual out-of-pocket costs of gathering information and the reasonable value of the landlord's time, with a maximum cap of $30 per applicant, subject to annual CPI adjustments.

Housing providers must evaluate the aggregate income of all persons residing together using the same standards applied to married persons.
For tenants with government rent subsidies, housing providers must base financial or income eligibility standards only on the portion of rent the tenant is responsible for paying.
For tenants with government rent subsidies, housing providers must allow applicants to provide alternative evidence of their ability to pay rent instead of relying solely on credit history.
Landlords must provide 30 days' written advance notice for rent increases of less than 10%.

If a residential rental property is re-rented within five years after a no-fault eviction under specific sections, the landlord must first offer to lease the unit back to the displaced tenant if the tenant timely requested it in writing and provided contact information.

Prior to making a buyout offer, landlords must provide each tenant a written disclosure stating their right not to enter into the agreement, consult an attorney, refuse future offers, and receive relocation assistance, among other mandated notices.
A landlord is prohibited from terminating a residential tenancy without establishing at-fault or no-fault just cause as defined by the ordinance.

A landlord of a residential rental property subject to this Division must provide written notice in no less than 12-point font regarding rent limits, local just cause termination rules, and senior or disabled tenant protections, and include a copy of the Tenant Protection Guide.

For no-fault just cause terminations, landlords must provide relocation assistance either via direct payment equal to two months of actual rent (or three months if the tenant is a senior or disabled) or through an equivalent rent waiver for the final months of tenancy.

Buyout agreements must be in writing, provide a copy to each tenant at signing, include specific bold statutory notices in at least 14-point font, be provided in translated versions if negotiations occurred in a non-English language, and be for an amount greater than the required relocation assistance.
Landlords are prohibited from retaliating against a tenant for exercising any right provided by or seeking enforcement of the division.
Any buyout agreement for less than the amount of relocation assistance owed to the tenant violates the division and is void.

Compliance with municipal rent control regulations is entirely voluntary and uncoerced after six months from the date of initial adoption, and property owners may decline to have their property subjected to the regulation.

Municipal rent control regulations cannot include the regulation of occupancy, services, evictions, condominium conversion, or removal of properties, and cannot apply to units owned by someone owning less than ten rental units or units with a fair market rent exceeding $400.

A municipality adopting rent control must compensate owners of rent-controlled units for the difference between the unit's fair market rent and its below-market rent-controlled rent using the municipality's general funds.

Cities and towns are prohibited from enacting, maintaining, or enforcing rent control of any kind, unless they accept Chapter 40P and adopt voluntary regulations meeting specific statutory conditions.

Estates at will may be determined by either party by giving three months' notice in writing, or an interval equal to the payment period or thirty days (whichever is longer) if rent is payable at periods of less than three months.

In case of neglect or refusal to pay rent, a fourteen days' notice to quit in writing is sufficient to determine the tenancy, provided that a tenant who has not received a similar notice within the preceding twelve months may cure the default by paying or tendering the full amount of rent due within ten days of receipt.

At or prior to the commencement of any tenancy, a lessor or agent may not require payments exceeding the first full month's rent, last full month's rent, a security deposit equal to the first month's rent, and the purchase and installation cost for a key and lock.

If a lessor fails to properly deposit security funds, transfer them to a successor, or return them to the tenant, the tenant is entitled to damages equal to three times the security deposit amount plus 5% interest, court costs, and attorney's fees.
Any lease provision that conflicts with the security deposit requirements or attempts to waive tenant rights under this section is void and unenforceable as a matter of public policy.
The security deposit provisions do not apply to vacation or recreational rentals with a duration of 100 days or less.

Landlords are prohibited from threatening or taking reprisals against residential tenants for reporting code violations, joining a tenants' union, or pursuing legal rights. Receipt of a notice of termination, rent increase, or substantial alteration in tenancy terms within six months of such tenant activity creates a rebuttable presumption of reprisal.
Any waiver of the statutory protections against landlord reprisals contained in any lease or other rental agreement shall be void and unenforceable.
A licensed broker or salesperson may only collect a fee from the party (lessor or tenant) who originally engaged and entered into a contract with them.

A landlord must provide a specific form alongside any notice to quit for nonpayment of rent, which includes repayment agreements and information on rental assistance and legal rights. Courts cannot accept an eviction filing for nonpayment of rent without proof that this form was delivered to the tenant.

After a tenant has occupied a property for 12 months, the owner must have just cause to terminate the tenancy and must state that cause in the written notice.
If an owner terminates a tenancy for a no-fault just cause, they must provide relocation assistance equal to one month's rent or waive the final month's rent.
After a tenant has occupied a property for 12 months (or 24 months if only one tenant has occupied it), a landlord must provide a statement of cause in any notice to terminate a tenancy.

An owner of residential real property shall not increase the gross rental rate for a dwelling or unit by more than 5 percent plus the percentage change in the cost of living, or 10 percent, whichever is lower, over any 12-month period.
A landlord shall not demand or receive a security deposit in excess of one month's rent, in addition to the first month's rent.
Landlords must return the security deposit and provide an itemized statement of deductions within 21 calendar days after the tenant has vacated the premises.

Landlords or their successors who act in bad faith regarding the retention of a security deposit or the demand for replacement security may be liable for statutory damages of up to twice the amount of the security deposit, in addition to actual damages.
A lease or rental agreement is prohibited from including any provision that characterizes a security deposit as nonrefundable.

The application screening fee must not exceed the actual out-of-pocket costs of gathering information and the reasonable value of the landlord's time, with a maximum cap of $30 per applicant, subject to annual CPI adjustments.

Landlords may not charge a screening fee if they know or should know no unit is available, and may only charge if they offer a compliant screening process (either first-come-first-served or a full refund policy for non-selected applicants).
Housing providers must evaluate the aggregate income of all persons residing together using the same standards applied to married persons.
For tenants with government rent subsidies, housing providers must base financial or income eligibility standards only on the portion of rent the tenant is responsible for paying.
For tenants with government rent subsidies, housing providers must allow applicants to provide alternative evidence of their ability to pay rent instead of relying solely on credit history.

Landlords must provide 30 days' written advance notice for rent increases of less than 10%.

A landlord or their agent may not charge an application or similar fee to lease or sublease a residential rental property that exceeds $50, subject to annual CPI adjustments.
No residential landlord may evict or fail to renew a lease, whether written or oral, without good cause, and the landlord must prove in court that grounds for eviction exist.
When a building is converted to a condominium, cooperative, or fee simple ownership, rents may not be increased solely to cover costs resulting from the conversion.
Landlords converting properties to condominiums or cooperatives must serve a three-year Notice to Quit before filing for eviction.
Landlords are allowed to charge the tenant for the cost of the credit report and may request reasonable rental application fees or employment verification.

A landlord may file an eviction suit if a tenant fails to pay a rent increase, provided the rent increase is not unconscionable and complies with all other laws or municipal ordinances, including rent control, and a Notice to Quit is served at least one month prior.
Landlords may evict for habitual late payment of rent after serving a Notice to Cease and a one-month Notice to Quit.
Tenants evicted for illegal occupancy are entitled to relocation assistance equal to six times their monthly rent, payable by the landlord at least five days before removal.

Certain senior citizens and recipients of specific governmental pensions, disability benefits, or assistance must be given a five-business-day grace period for rent due on the first of the month without delinquency or late charges assessed.
The maximum security deposit a landlord can collect from a tenant cannot exceed one and one-half times one month's rent.

Landlords and rental agencies are prohibited from refusing to rent or discriminating in housing units based on race, creed, color, national origin, ancestry, sex, marital status, civil union status, domestic partnership status, familial status, affectional or sexual orientation, gender identity or expression, mental and physical disability, nationality, or source of lawful income.

Landlords receiving security deposit money for ten or less units must deposit the funds in an insured bank or savings and loan association located in New Jersey in an interest-bearing account. Landlords with 10 or more units have the option of investing in an insured money market fund or a variable rate account in a New Jersey bank. All interest or earnings belong to the tenant and must be paid in cash or credited toward rent.

Within 30 days after the termination of a tenancy, a landlord must return the security deposit plus interest less allowable deductions. If a landlord fails to return the deposit within 30 days or wrongfully withholds an amount, the tenant may sue for double the amount plus court costs and reasonable attorney's fees.

When a new owner of a foreclosed property makes a bona fide monetary offer to induce a tenant to vacate, they are prohibited from using pressure tactics, including increasing rent in excess of any applicable rent control ordinance or, if not subject to rent control, imposing an unreasonable or unconscionable rent increase.
Newly constructed multiple dwellings are exempt from any local rent control ordinances for a period of 30 years following completion of construction.
Landlords may evict tenants who refuse reasonable, substantial changes to lease terms upon expiration, provided a one-month Notice to Quit is served.

Unknown: owner type is not in the supplied data. Landlords of residential rental properties, excluding owner-occupied two or three-family dwellings, motels, hotels, or transient/seasonal units, must have good cause to refuse to renew a lease.

Landlords are prohibited from evicting, altering lease terms, or refusing to renew a lease in reprisal for a tenant exercising civil rights, such as enforcing lease rights or complaining to government authorities.

Landlords seeking to permanently retire a building from residential use must serve a Notice to Quit at least 18 months prior to filing for eviction, and no action may be taken until the lease expires.

Landlords are prohibited from discriminating against tenants or purchasers based on their source of lawful income or source of lawful rent or mortgage payment, including the use of Section 8 HUD vouchers.

After a tenant has occupied a property for 12 months, the owner must have just cause to terminate the tenancy and must state that cause in the written notice.

After a tenant has occupied a property for 12 months (or 24 months if only one tenant has occupied it), a landlord must provide a statement of cause in any notice to terminate a tenancy.

Landlords must return the security deposit and provide an itemized statement of deductions within 21 calendar days after the tenant has vacated the premises.

Landlords or their successors who act in bad faith regarding the retention of a security deposit or the demand for replacement security may be liable for statutory damages of up to twice the amount of the security deposit, in addition to actual damages.

The application screening fee must not exceed the actual out-of-pocket costs of gathering information and the reasonable value of the landlord's time, with a maximum cap of $30 per applicant, subject to annual CPI adjustments.

Landlords may not charge a screening fee if they know or should know no unit is available, and may only charge if they offer a compliant screening process (either first-come-first-served or a full refund policy for non-selected applicants).

For tenants with government rent subsidies, housing providers must base financial or income eligibility standards only on the portion of rent the tenant is responsible for paying.
For tenants with government rent subsidies, housing providers must allow applicants to provide alternative evidence of their ability to pay rent instead of relying solely on credit history.

Landlords are prohibited from terminating tenancies without just cause and must provide relocation assistance for no-fault evictions.

All notices to terminate a tenancy for rental units subject to the RSO must be filed with the Los Angeles Housing Department within three business days of service on the tenant.
A landlord may collect 1/12 of 50% of the annual Systematic Code Enforcement Fee from the tenant of the rental unit per month.
Landlords must provide 30 days' written advance notice for rent increases of less than 10%.
Landlords of units subject to the Rent Stabilization Ordinance are limited to an annual rent increase of 3% for the period of July 1, 2025, through June 30, 2026.
Beginning February 2, 2026, landlords are prohibited from including any additional percentage increase for utilities in the rent.

Landlords may elect to pay monetary relocation benefits through an escrow account established within the required 15-day period, which must disburse funds for actual relocation expenses within three working days of receiving a request.

Compliance with municipal rent control regulations is entirely voluntary and uncoerced after six months from the date of initial adoption, and property owners may decline to have their property subjected to the regulation.

Municipal rent control regulations cannot include the regulation of occupancy, services, evictions, condominium conversion, or removal of properties, and cannot apply to units owned by someone owning less than ten rental units or units with a fair market rent exceeding $400.

A municipality adopting rent control must compensate owners of rent-controlled units for the difference between the unit's fair market rent and its below-market rent-controlled rent using the municipality's general funds.

Cities and towns are prohibited from enacting, maintaining, or enforcing rent control of any kind, unless they accept Chapter 40P and adopt voluntary regulations meeting specific statutory conditions.

Estates at will may be determined by either party by giving three months' notice in writing, or an interval equal to the payment period or thirty days (whichever is longer) if rent is payable at periods of less than three months.

In case of neglect or refusal to pay rent, a fourteen days' notice to quit in writing is sufficient to determine the tenancy, provided that a tenant who has not received a similar notice within the preceding twelve months may cure the default by paying or tendering the full amount of rent due within ten days of receipt.

At or prior to the commencement of any tenancy, a lessor or agent may not require payments exceeding the first full month's rent, last full month's rent, a security deposit equal to the first month's rent, and the purchase and installation cost for a key and lock.

If a lessor fails to properly deposit security funds, transfer them to a successor, or return them to the tenant, the tenant is entitled to damages equal to three times the security deposit amount plus 5% interest, court costs, and attorney's fees.
Any lease provision that conflicts with the security deposit requirements or attempts to waive tenant rights under this section is void and unenforceable as a matter of public policy.
The security deposit provisions do not apply to vacation or recreational rentals with a duration of 100 days or less.

Unknown: owner type is not in the supplied data. A housing provider is prohibited from inquiring about an applicant's criminal record or requiring an application that includes such inquiries until after a conditional offer of housing has been made.

Unknown: owner type is not in the supplied data. Housing providers are prohibited from evaluating applicants based on arrests not resulting in conviction, expunged convictions, pardoned convictions, vacated convictions, juvenile adjudications, or sealed records.

Unknown: owner type is not in the supplied data. Housing providers are prohibited from requiring applicants to submit to drug or alcohol tests or requesting consent to obtain information from drug abuse treatment facilities.
A landlord or their agent may not charge an application or similar fee to lease or sublease a residential rental property that exceeds $50, subject to annual CPI adjustments.
No residential landlord may evict or fail to renew a lease, whether written or oral, without good cause, and the landlord must prove in court that grounds for eviction exist.
When a building is converted to a condominium, cooperative, or fee simple ownership, rents may not be increased solely to cover costs resulting from the conversion.
Landlords converting properties to condominiums or cooperatives must serve a three-year Notice to Quit before filing for eviction.
Landlords are allowed to charge the tenant for the cost of the credit report and may request reasonable rental application fees or employment verification.

A landlord may file an eviction suit if a tenant fails to pay a rent increase, provided the rent increase is not unconscionable and complies with all other laws or municipal ordinances, including rent control, and a Notice to Quit is served at least one month prior.
Landlords may evict for habitual late payment of rent after serving a Notice to Cease and a one-month Notice to Quit.
Tenants evicted for illegal occupancy are entitled to relocation assistance equal to six times their monthly rent, payable by the landlord at least five days before removal.

Certain senior citizens and recipients of specific governmental pensions, disability benefits, or assistance must be given a five-business-day grace period for rent due on the first of the month without delinquency or late charges assessed.
The maximum security deposit a landlord can collect from a tenant cannot exceed one and one-half times one month's rent.

Landlords and rental agencies are prohibited from refusing to rent or discriminating in housing units based on race, creed, color, national origin, ancestry, sex, marital status, civil union status, domestic partnership status, familial status, affectional or sexual orientation, gender identity or expression, mental and physical disability, nationality, or source of lawful income.

Landlords receiving security deposit money for ten or less units must deposit the funds in an insured bank or savings and loan association located in New Jersey in an interest-bearing account. Landlords with 10 or more units have the option of investing in an insured money market fund or a variable rate account in a New Jersey bank. All interest or earnings belong to the tenant and must be paid in cash or credited toward rent.

Within 30 days after the termination of a tenancy, a landlord must return the security deposit plus interest less allowable deductions. If a landlord fails to return the deposit within 30 days or wrongfully withholds an amount, the tenant may sue for double the amount plus court costs and reasonable attorney's fees.

When a new owner of a foreclosed property makes a bona fide monetary offer to induce a tenant to vacate, they are prohibited from using pressure tactics, including increasing rent in excess of any applicable rent control ordinance or, if not subject to rent control, imposing an unreasonable or unconscionable rent increase.
Newly constructed multiple dwellings are exempt from any local rent control ordinances for a period of 30 years following completion of construction.
Landlords may evict tenants who refuse reasonable, substantial changes to lease terms upon expiration, provided a one-month Notice to Quit is served.

Unknown: owner type is not in the supplied data. Landlords of residential rental properties, excluding owner-occupied two or three-family dwellings, motels, hotels, or transient/seasonal units, must have good cause to refuse to renew a lease.

Landlords are prohibited from evicting, altering lease terms, or refusing to renew a lease in reprisal for a tenant exercising civil rights, such as enforcing lease rights or complaining to government authorities.

Landlords seeking to permanently retire a building from residential use must serve a Notice to Quit at least 18 months prior to filing for eviction, and no action may be taken until the lease expires.

Landlords are prohibited from discriminating against tenants or purchasers based on their source of lawful income or source of lawful rent or mortgage payment, including the use of Section 8 HUD vouchers.

Compliance with municipal rent control regulations is entirely voluntary and uncoerced after six months from the date of initial adoption, and property owners may decline to have their property subjected to the regulation.

Municipal rent control regulations cannot include the regulation of occupancy, services, evictions, condominium conversion, or removal of properties, and cannot apply to units owned by someone owning less than ten rental units or units with a fair market rent exceeding $400.

A municipality adopting rent control must compensate owners of rent-controlled units for the difference between the unit's fair market rent and its below-market rent-controlled rent using the municipality's general funds.

Cities and towns are prohibited from enacting, maintaining, or enforcing rent control of any kind, unless they accept Chapter 40P and adopt voluntary regulations meeting specific statutory conditions.

Estates at will may be determined by either party by giving three months' notice in writing, or an interval equal to the payment period or thirty days (whichever is longer) if rent is payable at periods of less than three months.

In case of neglect or refusal to pay rent, a fourteen days' notice to quit in writing is sufficient to determine the tenancy, provided that a tenant who has not received a similar notice within the preceding twelve months may cure the default by paying or tendering the full amount of rent due within ten days of receipt.

At or prior to the commencement of any tenancy, a lessor or agent may not require payments exceeding the first full month's rent, last full month's rent, a security deposit equal to the first month's rent, and the purchase and installation cost for a key and lock.

If a lessor fails to properly deposit security funds, transfer them to a successor, or return them to the tenant, the tenant is entitled to damages equal to three times the security deposit amount plus 5% interest, court costs, and attorney's fees.
Any lease provision that conflicts with the security deposit requirements or attempts to waive tenant rights under this section is void and unenforceable as a matter of public policy.
The security deposit provisions do not apply to vacation or recreational rentals with a duration of 100 days or less.

Landlords are prohibited from threatening or taking reprisals against residential tenants for reporting code violations, joining a tenants' union, or pursuing legal rights. Receipt of a notice of termination, rent increase, or substantial alteration in tenancy terms within six months of such tenant activity creates a rebuttable presumption of reprisal.
Any waiver of the statutory protections against landlord reprisals contained in any lease or other rental agreement shall be void and unenforceable.
A licensed broker or salesperson may only collect a fee from the party (lessor or tenant) who originally engaged and entered into a contract with them.

A landlord must provide a specific form alongside any notice to quit for nonpayment of rent, which includes repayment agreements and information on rental assistance and legal rights. Courts cannot accept an eviction filing for nonpayment of rent without proof that this form was delivered to the tenant.

Cities and towns are prohibited from enacting, maintaining, or enforcing rent control of any kind, unless they accept Chapter 40P and adopt voluntary regulations meeting specific statutory conditions.

Estates at will may be determined by either party by giving three months' notice in writing, or an interval equal to the payment period or thirty days (whichever is longer) if rent is payable at periods of less than three months.

At or prior to the commencement of any tenancy, a lessor or agent may not require payments exceeding the first full month's rent, last full month's rent, a security deposit equal to the first month's rent, and the purchase and installation cost for a key and lock.

Any lease provision that conflicts with the security deposit requirements or attempts to waive tenant rights under this section is void and unenforceable as a matter of public policy.
The security deposit provisions do not apply to vacation or recreational rentals with a duration of 100 days or less.

Landlords are prohibited from threatening or taking reprisals against residential tenants for reporting code violations, joining a tenants' union, or pursuing legal rights. Landlords may not request or receive a percentage rent increase greater than 5% or the percentage difference in the consumer price index between three months prior to lease expiration and three months prior to lease commencement, whichever is less.

The maximum security deposit a landlord can collect from a tenant cannot exceed one and one-half times one month's rent.
